title: HALT Fentanyl Act
official_title: An Act to amend the Controlled Substances Act with respect to the scheduling of fentanyl-related substances, and for other purposes.
summary: The HALT Fentanyl Act permanently places all fentanyl-related substances as a class into Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act, subjecting them to the same quantity-based mandatory minimum penalties that apply to fentanyl analogues under existing law. The law also creates a faster registration process for researchers who want to study Schedule I substances, including fentanyl, by allowing some research to begin as soon as 30 days after notifying the Attorney General.
brief: Permanently schedules all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I drugs and imposes the same mandatory minimum penalties as fentanyl, while creating an expedited process for researchers to study Schedule I substances.

top_lines.headline: Class Scheduling of Fentanyl Variants
subs: Any substance structurally related to fentanyl by one of five defined chemical modifications is permanently placed in Schedule I
Includes salts, isomers, and salts of isomers of any qualifying fentanyl-related substance
Attorney General may publish a Federal Register list of qualifying substances; unlisted substances still qualify if they meet the structural definition

top_lines.headline: Criminal Penalties for Fentanyl Variants
subs: Offenses involving fentanyl-related substances now trigger the same quantity-based mandatory minimums that apply to fentanyl analogues
The specific quantity thresholds for each mandatory minimum tier are set by cross-reference to the existing analogue provisions in Section 401(b)(1) and are not restated in the bill
Importation and exportation penalties under the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act also updated to include fentanyl-related substances

top_lines.headline: Research Registration Reforms
subs: Researchers already registered for Schedule I or II research may begin fentanyl-related research 30 days after notifying the Attorney General
New researchers without prior registration receive a registration decision within 45 days of submitting a notice
Single registration now permitted for related research sites in the same city or county under the same institution

likelihoodReason: Signed into law on July 16, 2025, as Public Law 119-26. The bill passed with bipartisan support in both chambers.

items.main: Names the Act the “Halt All Lethal Trafficking of Fentanyl Act” (the “HALT Fentanyl Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Class Scheduling of Fentanyl-Related Substances

items.main: Permanently adds a new category (e) to Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act covering any substance structurally related to fentanyl by one of five defined chemical modifications.
items.detail: The five structural modification criteria are: replacement of the phenethyl group's phenyl portion with any monocycle; substitution on the phenethyl group; substitution on the piperidine ring; replacement of the aniline ring with an aromatic monocycle; or replacement of the N-propionyl group with another acyl group. A substance is excluded from the class if it is already controlled under another schedule or expressly listed elsewhere.

items.main: Creates an alternative registration process for researchers conducting studies on Schedule I substances that are the subject of an investigational new drug exemption or funded by the Departments of Health and Human Services, Defense, or Veterans Affairs.
items.detail: Researchers already holding a Schedule I or II registration may proceed 30 days after sending notice to the Attorney General. New researchers without prior registration receive a decision — either a registration or an order to show cause — within 45 days. Researchers may continue studying a substance that is newly added to Schedule I while their registration application is pending, provided a registration application is submitted within 90 days of the scheduling action; the research may continue until the applicant withdraws the application or the Attorney General serves an order to show cause.

items.main: Allows registered researchers to perform small-quantity manufacturing activities — including creating extracts, tinctures, oils, solutions, and dosage forms — without obtaining a separate manufacturing registration.
items.detail: The activities must be within the scope stated in the researcher's notification or research protocol. Multiple staff at a single institution may conduct research under one researcher's registration without each obtaining a separate registration, provided the lead registered researcher notifies the Attorney General of each staff member's name and position.

sections.label: Section 4 — Technical Correction On Controlled Substances Dispensing

items.main: Makes technical corrections to Public Law 117-328 (division FF) provisions on controlled-substances dispensing, replacing internal cross-references from section “303(g)” to “303(h)” of the Controlled Substances Act, effective as if included in that enactment.
items.detail: Corrects sections 1252(a), 1262, and 1263(b) of division FF of Public Law 117-328 (codified at 21 U.S.C. 822-824, 829a and 42 U.S.C. provisions).

items.main: Directs the Attorney General to issue rules implementing the Act within 6 months of enactment, which may be issued as interim final rules that take effect immediately without a good-cause showing.
items.detail: Interim final rules must give interested persons an opportunity to comment and request a hearing; the Attorney General then issues a final rule under section 553 of title 5, U.S. Code.

items.main: Amends the mandatory minimum penalty provisions of the Controlled Substances Act and the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act to include fentanyl-related substances alongside fentanyl analogues.
items.detail: Under Section 401(b)(1)(A)(vi) and (B)(vi), offenses involving fentanyl-related substances now trigger the same quantity-based mandatory minimums as offenses involving fentanyl analogues. The specific quantity thresholds for each tier are set by cross-reference to those existing analogue provisions and are not restated in the bill text. Parallel amendments apply to importation and exportation offenses.

items.main: Provides that the Act's amendments apply beginning on the date of enactment regardless of when the section 5 rules are finalized, and includes a rule of construction and a sense of Congress.
items.detail: The rule of construction bars treating the amendments as evidence that, for pre-enactment conduct, a fentanyl-related substance is not an analogue under 21 U.S.C. 841(b)(1) and 960(b). The sense of Congress agrees with the Controlled Substances Act interpretation in United States v. McCray, 346 F. Supp. 3d 363 (W.D.N.Y. 2018).

underreported.summary: States that the bill's class scheduling amendment to penalty provisions may not be construed as evidence that, before enactment, a fentanyl-related substance was not already an analogue of fentanyl under existing law.
underreported.why_unreported: This provision preserves the government's ability to prosecute pre-enactment conduct involving fentanyl-related substances under prior analogue theory, meaning the bill's penalty framework extends backward in time through its rule of construction, not just forward. The bill title and stated purpose focus on prospective scheduling.

underreported.summary: Requires the Attorney General to publicly disclose on the Drug Enforcement Administration website when a particular Schedule I substance is subject to different research application criteria than other Schedule I substances, including the criteria and how they differ.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's primary research reform focuses on expediting approvals, but this transparency provision separately addresses situations where the Attorney General is applying non-standard criteria to specific substances, which may affect which substances researchers can practically access even with the new expedited process.

gaps: The bill permanently places fentanyl-related substances in Schedule I but does not establish any mechanism for de-scheduling a substance if it is later found to have accepted medical use, which is one of the criteria for Schedule I classification.

The expedited research registration process applies only to research funded by HHS, DOD, or VA, or involving an investigational new drug application — it does not apply to privately funded academic research outside those categories.

The bill imposes the same mandatory minimums on fentanyl-related substances as on fentanyl analogues but does not address the quantity thresholds used to distinguish between the two mandatory minimum tiers, which are set by cross-reference to existing analogue provisions and may not match the actual potency of all covered substances.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Obernolte
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, opioid overdoses have become an epidemic in this country. Last year, over 100,000 Americans lost their lives to overdose, and fentanyl poisoning is the driving force behind that. Mr. Speaker, it is not just the country at large that has experienced this problem. In my own district, we have seen an over 1,000 percent increase in the rate of fentanyl poisoning and deaths.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzgerald
featured_quotes.text: This is a historic moment, Mr. Speaker. House Republicans are delivering on a promise to stop the flow of deadly fentanyl that, for years, has been flooding our communities and, tragically, tearing families apart. Today, drug overdose is the leading cause of accidental death across the country, and fentanyl-driven overdoses are the leading cause of death for American adults between 18 and 45 years of age. That is because it is cheap to make, easy to transport, and so potent. Just a few milligrams can be lethal.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Joyce
featured_quotes.text: This bipartisan bill will save lives by providing critical tools for law enforcement to combat the ongoing opioid crisis across our country. Thousands of Americans continue to die each year from fentanyl overdoses, and Ohio has been particularly hard-hit by the epidemic. Prior to the temporary rescheduling in 2018, fentanyl-related substances could only be controlled individually, allowing cartel chemists to easily create new uncontrolled compounds.

added: Schedule I class designation for all fentanyl-related substances meeting structural modification criteria
Expedited 30-day notice-based research registration for researchers already holding a Schedule I or II registration
45-day decision deadline for new researcher registration applications involving qualifying Schedule I research
Single-registration option for related research sites in the same city or county under the same institution
Authorization for registered researchers to perform small-quantity manufacturing without a separate manufacturing registration
Continuation authority for researchers studying substances newly added to Schedule I while applications are pending
modified: Controlled Substances Act Section 401(b)(1)(A)(vi) and (B)(vi): mandatory minimums extended to fentanyl-related substances
Controlled Substances Import and Export Act Section 1010(b)(1)(F) and (2)(F): import/export penalties extended to fentanyl-related substances
Controlled Substances Act Section 302(e): single registration permitted for related research sites under same institution in same city or county
